Toxicology Chapter 178

Atypical and Serotonergic Antidepressants

This chapter is organized around the ED decisions that change care: delayed seizures with bupropion, trazodone hypotension/QT risk, SSRI/SNRI ECG and seizure risk, and recognition of serotonin syndrome.

Board frame: do not manage these drugs as one generic antidepressant overdose. The dangerous pattern depends on agent, formulation, coingestants, ECG, seizure history, neuromuscular exam, and temperature.
Tintinalli source

Tintinalli Table 178-1. Atypical antidepressants

Use this table as the agent map before separating bupropion, mirtazapine, trazodone, vilazodone, and vortioxetine into their clinical risk patterns.

Bupropion

Bupropion is the atypical antidepressant that most often turns a quiet-looking ingestion into a delayed seizure problem. It is structurally stimulant-like and lowers seizure threshold; large or extended-release ingestions can produce agitation, tremor, hallucinations, tachycardia, QRS/QT changes, shock, and recurrent seizures hours after arrival.

Extended-release bupropion needs prolonged observation because symptoms can be delayed after an initially reassuring exam. ED care starts with airway readiness, IV access, cardiac monitoring, glucose/electrolytes, and aggressive benzodiazepine treatment for agitation or seizures. Sodium bicarbonate is reasonable when QRS widening suggests sodium-channel blockade physiology; magnesium treats torsades.

Tintinalli source

Tintinalli Table 178-2. Treatment of bupropion overdose

Placed inside the bupropion section because this is the actual bupropion treatment flow, not a drug-dose appendix item.

Trap: one normal early ECG or a calm early exam does not clear a large sustained-release bupropion ingestion.

Trazodone

Trazodone overdose is usually a sedation and vascular-tone problem, but severe cases can cause coma, respiratory depression from coingestants, orthostatic or persistent hypotension, QT prolongation, torsades, and priapism. Its alpha-1 blockade explains why fluids may not be enough in large ingestions.

Treatment is supportive: airway protection when needed, fluids for hypotension, direct-acting vasopressors such as norepinephrine for refractory shock, ECG monitoring, magnesium for torsades, and observation until mental status and hemodynamics are stable. Priapism is a time-sensitive urologic complication and should not be buried under general overdose care.

SSRIs

Most isolated SSRI ingestions are benign compared with older antidepressants, but the ED still has to screen for dose, formulation, coingestants, serotonin toxicity, and ECG risk. Citalopram and escitalopram are the board-relevant exceptions because they can cause QT prolongation and torsades at high doses.

Management is supportive care, observation, ECG monitoring when the agent or dose warrants it, benzodiazepines for agitation/seizures, sodium bicarbonate if a prolonged QRS appears, and magnesium for torsades. The treatment threshold rises quickly when the exam shows clonus, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, agitation, or hyperthermia.

SNRIs

SNRIs, especially venlafaxine and desvenlafaxine, behave less benignly than many isolated SSRI ingestions. In overdose they can produce nausea, agitation, diaphoresis, hypertension, tachycardia, seizures, QRS/QT abnormalities, and serotonin syndrome. Large venlafaxine ingestions can deteriorate after an initially stable period.

ED management parallels SSRI care but with a lower threshold for seizure and cardiovascular monitoring: benzodiazepines for agitation/seizures, IV fluids and vasopressors for shock, sodium bicarbonate for significant QRS widening, magnesium for torsades, and prolonged observation when extended-release ingestion or severe symptoms are present.

Serotonin Syndrome

Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis caused by excess serotonergic activity. The high-yield pattern is clonus plus hyperreflexia, often with agitation, tremor, diaphoresis, diarrhea, tachycardia, hypertension, and hyperthermia after a serotonergic medication change, overdose, or interaction.

The distinction from neuroleptic malignant syndrome matters: serotonin syndrome is usually faster and hyperreflexic with clonus, while NMS is slower with lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia. Severe serotonin syndrome is a muscle-activity emergency; antipyretics alone do not work because the heat is generated by rigidity and clonus.

Treatment starts with stopping serotonergic agents, supportive care, IV fluids, benzodiazepines, and active cooling. Moderate to severe cases may receive enteral cyproheptadine. Life-threatening hyperthermia requires aggressive sedation, intubation, neuromuscular paralysis, and ICU-level cooling and monitoring.

Drug Dose Reference

This section is only a quick recap after the topic-specific treatment sections above. It should never be the only place where treatment logic or treatment tables appear.

ProblemED treatment anchorBoard caution
Bupropion seizures/agitationBenzodiazepines; airway readiness; ICU/telemetry for severe or extended-release ingestionDelayed and recurrent seizures are the disposition trap.
QRS wideningSodium bicarbonate bolus and reassessmentUse ECG response and hemodynamics, not drug name alone.
Torsades/QT riskMagnesium sulfate, electrolyte correction, telemetryCitalopram/escitalopram and trazodone matter here.
Refractory hypotensionFluids then direct-acting vasopressor such as norepinephrineTrazodone alpha blockade can require pressors.
Serotonin syndromeStop agents, benzodiazepines, cooling; cyproheptadine enterally for moderate/severe casesSevere hyperthermia needs paralysis/intubation, not antipyretics alone.

Key Points

Bupropion

Delayed seizures, QRS/QT changes, and shock define risk.

Trazodone

Sedation plus hypotension and QT effects; think direct vasopressors when fluids fail.

SSRIs/SNRIs

Most SSRIs are supportive-care cases, but citalopram/escitalopram and venlafaxine deserve ECG/seizure respect.

Serotonin syndrome

Clonus and hyperreflexia are the diagnosis handles; severe cases are cooling and paralysis emergencies.

Inline Assessment MCQs

Q1. A patient has a generalized seizure several hours after a large antidepressant ingestion and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QRS widening. Which exposure is most concerning?

A. Sertraline onlyIsolated SSRI overdose is usually milder and less seizure-prone than bupropion.
B. Bupropion extended releaseBupropion, especially extended-release, is strongly associated with delayed seizures and QRS/QT issues.
C. Mirtazapine onlyMirtazapine is usually sedating and less likely to cause severe seizures.
D. Trazodone onlyTrazodone can cause hypotension/QT effects, but delayed seizures point more strongly to bupropion.

Q2. Best initial ED approach for bupropion overdose with recurrent seizures?

A. Airway readiness, benzodiazepines, ECG monitoring, electrolytes, and toxicology/ICU involvementBupropion seizures can recur and deteriorate; supportive resuscitation and monitoring drive care.
B. FlumazenilFlumazenil can provoke seizures.
C. Naloxone aloneNaloxone does not treat bupropion toxicity.
D. Immediate discharge after one normal ECGDelayed seizures make early discharge unsafe.

Q3. Which trazodone toxicity pattern is board-relevant?

A. Pure cholinergic crisisNot the typical trazodone pattern.
B. MethemoglobinemiaNot typical.
C. Opioid toxidromeNot typical unless coingestion exists.
D. CNS depression, hypotension, and QT prolongationTrazodone overdose commonly centers on sedation, alpha blockade hypotension, and QT effects.

Q4. A trazodone overdose patient has persistent hypotension after fluids. Next best escalation?

A. Long-acting oral antihypertensiveThis worsens hypotension.
B. PhysostigmineNot indicated for trazodone shock.
C. Direct-acting vasopressor such as norepinephrineAlpha blockade can require direct vasopressors.
D. Forced diuresisForced diuresis does not clear trazodone.

Q5. Most isolated SSRI overdoses are managed with:

A. Supportive care and observation with ECG/serotonin-syndrome screening when indicatedMost SSRI ingestions are benign; screen for citalopram/escitalopram ECG risk and serotonin syndrome.
B. Routine hemodialysisSSRIs are not managed by routine dialysis.
C. Empiric sodium thiosulfateCyanide antidote is unrelated.
D. Charcoal at 24 hours for everyoneCharcoal is time/airway dependent, not universal.

Q6. Which SSRI exposure deserves particular ECG attention?

A. Fluoxetine at a therapeutic doseTherapeutic fluoxetine is not the ECG overdose trap.
B. Citalopram or escitalopram overdoseCitalopram/escitalopram overdoses are associated with QT prolongation and torsades risk.
C. Mirtazapine monotherapyNot an SSRI and usually less ECG-toxic.
D. Bupropion missed doseMissed dose is not overdose.

Q7. An SNRI overdose with severe hypertension, tachycardia, and seizures most strongly suggests:

A. Mild mirtazapine ingestionMirtazapine is usually milder/sedating.
B. Isolated trazodone sleepinessTrazodone is more hypotension/QT.
C. Ibuprofen toxicityNSAID toxicity does not fit.
D. Venlafaxine/desvenlafaxine toxicityVenlafaxine can cause sympathomimetic features, seizures, and cardiovascular toxicity.

Q8. Serotonin syndrome is most suggested by:

A. Lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia over daysThis favors NMS.
B. Pinpoint pupils and apneaThis favors opioid toxicity.
C. Clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia after serotonergic exposureClonus and hyperreflexia are key serotonin syndrome findings.
D. Isolated orthostatic hypotensionNot enough for serotonin syndrome.

Q9. First-line medication for agitation and tremor in serotonin syndrome is:

A. BenzodiazepinesBenzodiazepines reduce agitation and muscle activity.
B. Haloperidol escalationDopamine antagonists can complicate hyperthermic toxidromes.
C. FlumazenilCan provoke seizures.
D. Beta blocker monotherapyDoes not treat the core syndrome and can be risky.

Q10. Severe serotonin syndrome with temperature 41 C and rigidity requires:

A. Acetaminophen onlyAntipyretics do not stop muscle heat generation.
B. Aggressive sedation, active cooling, paralysis/intubation when needed, and ICU careSevere cases need rapid control of muscle activity and temperature.
C. Observation at homeUnsafe.
D. PhysostigmineNot appropriate.

Q11. Cyproheptadine is best described as:

A. An IV paralyticIt is not a paralytic.
B. A dialysis enhancerIt does not enhance dialysis.
C. A charcoal substituteIt is not decontamination.
D. An oral/enteral serotonin antagonist adjunct for moderate/severe serotonin syndromeCyproheptadine can be used as enteral adjunct after supportive care.

Q12. Which distinction favors serotonin syndrome over NMS?

A. Rapid onset with clonus and hyperreflexiaThis is the classic serotonin syndrome pattern.
B. Slow onset over days with lead-pipe rigidityFavors NMS.
C. Dopamine antagonist withdrawal onlyNot serotonin syndrome.
D. Normal neuromuscular examDoes not support diagnosis.

Q13. Drug Dose Reference should be used for:

A. Replacing treatment sectionsTreatment must be discussed in each topic.
B. Parking all treatment tables away from topicsTables belong next to topic.
C. Quick recap after full treatment discussionCorrect: it is only a quick dose recap.
D. Hiding the clinical algorithmWrong use.

Q14. Why are extended-release bupropion ingestions observed longer?

A. They cause immediate cyanide releaseNo cyanide.
B. Delayed absorption and delayed/recurrent seizuresDelayed seizures are the core risk.
C. They are removed by naloxoneNaloxone does not reverse bupropion.
D. They never cause symptomsFalse.

Q15. A patient taking linezolid plus an SSRI develops clonus and fever. Mechanism?

A. Opioid agonismNot opioid.
B. Anticholinergic blockade onlyDoes not explain clonus.
C. Lithium redistributionNot lithium.
D. Serotonergic excess from interacting agentsLinezolid has MAOI activity and can contribute to serotonin syndrome.

Q16. Which finding requires telemetry after antidepressant overdose?

A. QT prolongation or QRS wideningECG interval abnormalities drive monitored care.
B. Normal vitals and normal ECG after adequate observationMay support discharge depending scenario.
C. Remote tiny ingestion with no symptomsLower risk.
D. Mild nausea onlyNot enough alone.

Q17. Which seizure drug strategy is preferred in these toxicologic seizures?

A. Phenytoin first for allPhenytoin is not first-line for most toxicologic seizures.
B. No treatmentUnsafe.
C. Benzodiazepines firstCorrect.
D. More antidepressantWrong.

Q18. Which patient should not be cleared early?

A. Asymptomatic SSRI ingestion with normal ECG after adequate observationMay be reasonable if criteria met.
B. Large extended-release bupropion ingestion still within delayed seizure windowDelayed seizures make early clearance unsafe.
C. Tiny accidental mirtazapine ingestion with normal observationLikely lower risk.
D. Remote trazodone ingestion with normal vitals and ECGMay be lower risk after adequate observation.

Q19. What makes SNRI overdose different from most SSRI overdose?

A. No seizure risk everFalse.
B. Always requires dialysisNo.
C. Always produces opioid toxidromeNo.
D. More sympathomimetic/cardiovascular and seizure risk, especially venlafaxineCorrect.

Q20. Most important bedside endpoint in severe serotonin syndrome treatment is:

A. Stopping muscle activity and lowering core temperatureHyperthermia is generated by muscle activity.
B. Lowering fever with acetaminophen aloneNot enough.
C. Waiting for a serum serotonin levelNo useful ED serum serotonin test.
D. Forcing urine outputNot the main issue.

Q21. Which medication combination is high risk for serotonin syndrome?

A. Acetaminophen plus ibuprofenNo.
B. Insulin plus dextroseNo.
C. SSRI plus MAOI/linezolid/tramadol or multiple serotonergic agentsCorrect interaction pattern.
D. Albuterol plus ipratropiumNo.

Q22. For trazodone-related torsades, treat with:

A. Calcium carbonate orallyNot torsades care.
B. Magnesium sulfate and correction of electrolytesMagnesium is first-line for torsades.
C. NaloxoneNot opioid.
D. FomepizoleToxic alcohol antidote.

Q23. Which symptom cluster after SSRI overdose should trigger serotonin syndrome treatment rather than simple observation?

A. Clonus, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermiaThis is serotonin toxicity.
B. Mild nausea onlyUsually supportive observation.
C. Sleepiness with normal vitals onlyNot enough.
D. Normal neuromuscular examNot serotonin syndrome.

Q24. Which statement about mirtazapine overdose is most accurate?

A. It always causes fatal dysrhythmiaFalse.
B. It causes cyanide poisoningNo.
C. It always needs hemodialysisNo.
D. It is often sedating and supportive-care managed, but coingestions still matterCorrect.

Q25. Disposition after atypical/serotonergic antidepressant ingestion should consider:

A. Only the drug nameToo narrow.
B. Only one normal blood pressureInsufficient.
C. Formulation, time since ingestion, ECG, seizures, serotonin findings, coingestants, and symptom trendCorrect integrated disposition.
D. Urine drug screen aloneUDS is not enough.

Q26. Best overall ED summary for this chapter?

A. Risk-stratify by agent, formulation, ECG, seizure risk, and serotonin toxicity; treat supportively with targeted escalationCorrect chapter-level approach.
B. All antidepressant overdoses are benignBupropion, venlafaxine, citalopram, trazodone, and serotonin syndrome can be dangerous.
C. All need dialysisWrong.
D. All are treated with flumazenilDangerous and wrong.
